newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain bids soggy but proud farewell to HK.
newsitem.headline: Britain bids soggy but proud farewell to HK.

text.p: Britain bade a soggy but proud farewell on Monday to its last great colony, keeping a stiff upper lip through a tropical downpour on its final parade in Hong Kong.
It mattered not that the drumming rain at sunset nearly drowned out the words of Prince Charles, muted the plaintive bagpipe strains of the Lone Piper and slowed the dragon dancers.

This was the last great hurrah of a British Empire that once spanned the world and the 10,000 Hong Kong residents who won the right to be present stayed huddled under umbrellas in their seats until the last second.
"The rain was the best part of it. We're British after all," joked Nicola Walker, a seven-year resident of the colony. "I was so proud to be British tonight."

Sitting in the VIP section with Prince Charles, also soaked and under umbrellas, were Hong Kong's last governor Chris Patten, Prime Minister Tony Blair and former prime ministers Margaret Thatcher and Edward Heath who played key parts in negotiations that led to Hong Kong's return to China.

On the parade ground, true to tradition, the marching bands and skirling pipers bravely put on their last great show east of Suez without missing a beat or a step in an open-air stadium on Hong Kong harbour.
There were also fireworks and scenes told through song and dance of Hong Kong's past and present. The future was left untold.
It was one mile (two km) away at Possession Point that the Union Jack was first planted on Hong Kong soil 156 years ago, setting off all that was to follow.

Dressed in white naval uniform and wearing a ceremonial sword, Prince Charles delivered a message from his mother Queen Elizabeth, in which she said Hong Kong's future depended on implementation by Beijing of a 1984 Sino-British agreement.
Under the accord, Beijing promised Hong Kong would enjoy autonomy under a unique "one country, two systems" formula that allows capitalist Hong Kong to retain its freedoms for 50 years.
"Britain is part of Hong Kong's history and Hong Kong is part of Britain's history. We are also part of each other's future," the Queen's message said.
However the biggest applause of the two-hour ceremony was for Patten, Hong Kong's 28th and last governor, the man who guided the colony through its critical last five years.
Denounced by Beijing as a "whore" because of his tough negotiating stance on civil liberties, on this night he was among friends.
He declared Hong Kong's unshakeable destiny was that its own people would run its affairs. No dependent territory had ever achieved more prosperity, he said.
He wished Hong Kong well in "the challenging years ahead" as an autonomous Special Administrative Region of China.

"As British administration ends, we are, I believe, entitled to say that our own nation's contribution here was to provide the scaffolding that enabled the people of Hong Kong to ascend," Patten said.
At the end of his speech, he sat down and bowed his head, biting back tears as the crowd roared.

He had to stand and wave in acknowledgement before they quietened and a band struck up with the music of Edward Elgar, whose works are often seen as reflecting a sense of personal loss and imperial transience.
"We've done a darn good job. We can walk away with our heads held high," said Bruce Walker, a property agent who has lived in Hong Kong for seven years.

With the loss of the 6.4 million people of Hong Kong, Britain's colonial subjects shrink to a total of 180,000 people spread over 13 dependencies ranging from 61,000 in Bermuda to about 50 on tiny Pitcairn Island
